chapters.narration_en: A shopkeeper has a box of receipts and one question: which day of the week should she close? She cannot answer it by looking, because a person cannot hold a thousand rows in their head. So she does what every data person does. She lays the receipts out — gets the rows. She works out which ones she can trust. And then she answers the question. That is the whole job. Spreadsheets, SQL, Python, dashboards, machine learning — every tool in this film is a different way of doing those same three moves at a different scale. And the unglamorous middle move is most of the work. In a real week you will spend far more time discovering that Cairo, cairo and Cairo-with-a-trailing-space are three different cities to a computer than you will spend building anything clever. Here are six payments from NilePay, a mobile-money service we will follow all the way to the end. Four succeeded. Before I tell you the success rate — work it out.

chapters.narration_en: Seven movements. From nothing to a working machine — files, folders, the terminal, your first line of code. From code to structured data — variables, tables, SQL, keys, transactions. From one program to a software system — objects, tests, version control, APIs, networking, security. From one database to a data platform — pipelines, warehouses, DAGs, Spark, Kafka. From a platform to a real business — mobile money, near-real-time reporting, reconciliation, governance, disaster recovery. From analytics to AI — statistics, models, neural networks, attention, retrieval, agents. And finally, from lessons to evidence. One project runs through all seven. It starts as a folder and ends as a system you can defend in an interview. Every example uses the same fourteen fields, so knowledge compounds instead of resetting. Money is a decimal, never a float, because binary floating point cannot represent ten piastres exactly — and a rounding error in a payments platform is not a rounding error, it is a missing customer's money. Progress here is not measured in lessons finished. It is measured in things you can show.

chapters.narration_en: Before we start, learn the grammar. Four things will keep happening. First: anything that controls behaviour is drawn, not described. A stack, a queue, an offset, a retry budget — if it decides what happens next, you will see it on screen beside the thing it controls. Second: processes have a transport. Play, pause, step forward, step back, and a counter telling you where you are, because understanding a process means being able to stop it in the middle. Third: parameters have visible consequences. When a number moves, the picture redraws immediately — that is how you learn what a parameter actually does, rather than what its name suggests. Fourth, and most important: every mechanism is shown twice. Once working. Once broken. You will see a system that looks correct, then the hidden defect, then the trace, the root cause, the fix, and the same scene replayed to prove it recovered. That is not decoration. In real work, the thing you are paid for is the second half of that sequence. And regularly, before an animation plays, I will ask you to predict what happens. Answer out loud. Being wrong on purpose is the fastest way to learn.

chapters.narration_en: A computer does one thing, extremely fast, over and over: it fetches an instruction, decodes it, and executes it. Watch the pointer move — that is the whole machine. Data lives in two places and the difference decides most of your future performance problems. RAM is fast, addressed, and forgets everything the moment the program stops. Disk is slower and remembers. Reading from memory takes nanoseconds; reading from disk takes microseconds or milliseconds — and that gap is why a database keeps an index, why Spark caches, and why your program dies on a big file but works on a small one. Now, the smallest unit. A byte is eight switches, so it holds 256 different values. A number is a byte pattern. A letter is also a byte pattern — but only because we all agreed on which pattern means which letter. That agreement is called an encoding. In UTF-8, this four-letter word is five bytes long, because the accented character needs two. Every mysterious `UnicodeDecodeError` you will ever meet is that sentence, arriving as a crash.

chapters.title_en: Files, paths, processes and the terminal
chapters.teaches: what a file and a path are, what a process is, and why the terminal is a conversation.
labels_en: the first pipeline you will ever write
chapters.prediction: "The file is right there. Why did that fail?"

chapters.narration_en: A file is a run of bytes that has been given a name. A directory groups names into a tree. And a path is a set of directions through that tree — absolute if it starts at the root, relative if it starts wherever you happen to be standing. Almost every *file not found* in your career is a disagreement about where you are standing, not about whether the file exists. The terminal is where you have that conversation directly. You type one command, and something observable changes: the working directory, the filesystem, a process, or just some text on the screen. Watch the state change beside each command — that is the only way these are worth learning. Then the idea that makes Unix matter: standard output of one program can become standard input of the next. Count the failed rows without opening the file, without writing a program, in one line. That is a pipeline. We will meet Airflow in about thirty-five minutes and it will be the same idea with retries, a calendar and a user interface bolted on. And here is your first real error. Read it. It is not hostile — it is telling you precisely which assumption was wrong.

chapters.teaches: users and permissions, processes and signals, systemd services, journald, disk pressure, and the diagnosis path.

chapters.narration_en: Most data platforms run on Linux, so the difference between guessing and knowing on a bad night is this chapter. Permissions are not a wall, they are three questions asked in order: are you the owner, are you in the group, or are you neither? The kernel consults exactly one of those classes and then stops — which is why adding a group permission sometimes changes nothing at all. A process is a running program with its own memory and its own file handles. You ask it to stop with `SIGTERM`, which it may handle and clean up after. You force it with `SIGKILL`, which it cannot catch — and which is why a forced kill can leave a half-written file behind. Services are processes the machine manages for you, and here is the thing that matters on call: this unit is in a crash loop, but the cause is two services upstream of it. The first question on call is never *what broke*, it is *what broke first*. So read the log from the bottom up and find the earliest line that is not a consequence of something above it. And watch the disk: a full disk does not announce itself, it just makes everything else start failing strangely.

chapters.narration_en: In Python a variable is not a magic box. It is a name bound to a value, and the arrow between them is the whole idea — because in a few minutes two names are going to point at the same object and that will surprise you. Control flow is just a pointer walking a path. When a condition is true, watch which branch the pointer takes, and notice that the other branch is still there, dimmed, not deleted. A loop is the same pointer going round, and an accumulator is a value that survives the loop body — which is why it has to be created before the loop and not inside it. That single mistake accounts for a remarkable share of beginner bugs. A function is a calculation with a name. When you call one, a stack frame rises: the parameters bind to their arguments, the work happens inside that frame, and a value is returned as the frame disappears. Decomposition stops being an abstract virtue the moment you can see frames appearing and vanishing. Here are five ShopFlow orders. Three of them are delivered. Before the last iteration runs — what is the running total?

chapters.narration_en: Four containers, and you choose between them by the operation you do most, not by habit. A list keeps order. A dictionary maps a key to a value. A set enforces uniqueness. A tuple is a fixed record. Here is the one that costs people real time: checking whether something is in a list means walking the list — ten thousand comparisons for ten thousand items. The same check against a set is one hop, on average, because a set hashes the value straight to its location. Put that check inside a loop over another ten thousand rows and you have just built the difference between two seconds and five minutes. Next: data disappears when the program stops, unless you write it somewhere. CSV is rows and columns, flat and everywhere. JSON keeps nesting, which is why APIs speak it. And finally, environments — the least glamorous and most load-bearing idea here. A virtual environment keeps this project's dependencies away from every other project's. A `requirements.txt` records exactly what you installed. Without both, the sentence *"it works on my machine"* is not a joke, it is a bug report you cannot act on.

chapters.narration_en: Now the thing that separates people who read Python from people who can debug it. Two names can point at the same object. Change it through one name and the other name sees the change, because there was only ever one object. Look at the arrows, not the code. Here is the classic. A default argument is created once, when the function is defined — not once per call. So a mutable default quietly accumulates across every call your program ever makes, and the bug shows up hours later in data that looks almost right. Memory next. Building a list means holding everything at once; watch the memory bar climb until the process is killed. A generator produces one item at a time and holds one item at a time, so the bar stays flat over a file larger than your RAM. That is not an optimisation, it is the difference between a loader that survives production and one that does not. Finally, errors. An exception does not stop the program where it happened — it unwinds the stack, popping frames until something is willing to handle it. `finally` runs on the way past, which is how a file handle or a database connection gets closed even when everything has gone wrong.

chapters.narration_en: A test is an expected value written down where a machine can check it. Arrange, act, assert. And the run that matters is this one — the failing one. A test that has never failed has never proved anything; it might be asserting nothing at all. So: red, then green, then refactor with the test holding the behaviour still. When something breaks, the traceback is the most useful message you will ever be shown. Read it from the bottom: the last line is what went wrong, and the lines above it are the path that got there. Form one hypothesis. Test that hypothesis. Do not change three things at once, because then a passing run tells you nothing about which change was the fix. Git gives the project a memory: commits, branches, and diffs you can review. A merge conflict is not git failing — it is git refusing to guess, because two people rewrote the same region and only a human knows which version was intended. And the review itself is where a change becomes a shared decision: does it do what the ticket asked, does it handle the edge case, and can the next person understand it in six months. The artifact you keep from this chapter is not the code. It is a merged pull request containing a change, a test, and an explanation.

chapters.narration_en: Why not just keep the file? Because two people editing the same file at once means one of them loses. Because finding a row means reading every row. And because a file cannot stop you from writing nonsense into it. A database is the same grid with three additions. Types, so a date column cannot hold the word *maybe*. Keys, so every row has an identity and rows in one table can point at rows in another — a primary key identifies, a foreign key refers. And constraints, which are business rules turned into walls. `NOT NULL` says this fact is required. `UNIQUE` says this value identifies one thing. `CHECK` says the amount cannot be negative. A foreign key says you may not reference a customer who does not exist. Constraints are not decoration and they are not performance overhead you can skip — they are the only part of the system that is still enforcing the rule at three in the morning when nobody is reading the code. Keep an eye on this row: order ten-oh-seven points at customer 9, and customer 9 is not in the customers table. Nothing is stopping it yet. We will come back to it.

chapters.title_en: The query pipeline and the grain question

chapters.narration_en: SQL does not run in the order you write it. Watch. `FROM` first, because the engine needs rows before it can do anything. Then `JOIN`, and this is where the number of rows can explode or collapse. Then `WHERE` — and this is your cheapest win in the entire language, because every row eliminated now is a row the grouping never touches. Then `GROUP BY`, where rows collapse into one per group. Then `HAVING`, the group filter. Only now does `SELECT` run, and only now does the alias `revenue` come into existence — which is precisely why `WHERE` could not use it and `ORDER BY` can. Then `DISTINCT`, then `ORDER BY`, and `LIMIT` absolutely last. Watch the funnel: fourteen rows in, thirteen after the join drops the orphan, eleven after the filter, two groups out — gold and silver — and add them up: three thousand nine hundred and forty-eight fifty, the same total the cleaning chapter will reach from the other direction. Now the question that gets more candidates rejected than any syntax error. Before you write a single line, answer this: one row per *what*? One per order, one per customer, one per customer per day? Most broken dashboards are not broken syntax. They are a `SUM` computed at the wrong grain, which returns a perfectly confident number that is simply not the answer to the question that was asked. And `LIMIT 1` — did the engine save any work? It still had to produce and sort every group to know which one wins.

chapters.narration_en: Six join shapes, matched row by row. An inner join keeps rows that matched on both sides — and watch what it does here. Order ten-oh-seven points at customer 9, who does not exist, so the inner join removes the order entirely, and it does so silently. Your total is now wrong and nothing warned you. A left join keeps it, with nulls on the right. Now the failure that quietly inflates numbers across the industry. Six customers go in. Fifteen rows come out. More rows out than in is called fan-out, and it happens whenever the key you joined on is not unique on the other side. The grain silently changed from one row per customer to one row per order, so any customer-level number you sum now counts Amara four times. Every downstream `SUM` is larger than the truth. Windows are the opposite operation. `GROUP BY` collapses rows; a window function computes across a partition and still returns every row. Watch the partition boundary and the frame the function can actually see, sliding one row at a time. When two values tie, `ROW_NUMBER` still invents an order — which is exactly why you deduplicate with `ROW_NUMBER` and not with `RANK`. And finally, nulls. `NULL` is not a value, it is the absence of one, so comparing it to anything returns *unknown*, not false. `NOT IN` against a set containing a single null returns no rows at all — correctly, and catastrophically.

chapters.title_en: Transactions, isolation and deadlock
chapters.teaches: ACID, the four isolation levels and what each removes, locks, deadlock, MVCC.
chapters.prediction: "Both wrote. What is the balance now?"
chapters.callback: the concurrent file overwrite from CH-10.
chapters.artifact: a checkout transaction with a regression test.
chapters.narration_en: A transaction is a promise that a group of changes happens completely or not at all. Atomic: all or nothing. Consistent: constraints hold at the end. Isolated: concurrent work does not see your half-finished state. Durable: once committed, a crash cannot undo it. Here is why isolation exists. Both sessions read a balance of five hundred, both add to it, both write — and one of those updates has silently vanished. That is a lost update, and it is a data-loss bug that produces no error. Isolation is a dial, not a switch. Each level removes one anomaly and charges you for it: read committed removes dirty reads, repeatable read removes non-repeatable reads, serializable removes phantoms — and each step up costs concurrency. Now the one every interviewer asks about. Session A holds row one and wants row two. Session B holds row two and wants row one. Neither can proceed, and the wait graph has a cycle in it. The database does not hang; it detects the cycle and kills one session as the victim. The fix is not a bigger machine. Acquire locks in a consistent order, keep transactions short, and retry the victim with backoff.

chapters.title_en: Indexes, plans and the tuning loop
chapters.teaches: B-tree seeks, selectivity, sargability, reading `EXPLAIN`, write cost, pooling, and the discipline of one change at a time, measured in rows examined.
chapters.prediction: "The query returns half the table. Index or scan?"

chapters.narration_en: Tuning is a method, not a reflex. Reproduce, baseline, read the plan, form one hypothesis, make one change, measure, and check what you broke. And measure in rows examined, not milliseconds — wall-clock time moves between runs on a busy machine, while rows examined is exact. Here is the baseline: finding one customer reads twelve thousand five hundred pages. An index is a tree, and a seek is a walk down it. On the left, the full scan reads every page. On the right, three levels of B-tree reach the same row in three page reads — over a million rows. The height grows logarithmically, so ten times the data adds roughly one level, not ten times the work. That is the whole reason indexes matter. But an index is not free and it is not always right. Move the selectivity slider. When the query returns a handful of rows the seek wins overwhelmingly. When it returns most of the table, the scan wins again, because you are reading almost everything anyway and the index has only added a detour. Where exactly that crossover sits depends on the engine and on how the table is stored, which is why you measure rather than recite a percentage. Then sargability: wrap an indexed column in a function and the index becomes unusable, because the engine can no longer reason about the ordering. Rewrite it as a range and it works. Now read the plan properly. The row counts matter more than the operator names: when *estimated* and *actual* disagree by orders of magnitude, the planner made a good decision from bad information, and your fix is statistics, not another index. Finally, the cost you accepted. Every insert now writes twice — once to the table and once to the index — and every index you add is paid for on every write, forever. And performance is not only the database: a pool with sixty-seven requests per second of capacity, handed two hundred and sixty, forms a queue two hundred and eighty-nine deep, and the wait at the ninety-fifth percentile passes a second.

chapters.narration_en: Real data is broken, and knowing exactly *how* it is broken is a skill. Fifteen rows, eight genuine defects: a duplicated row, names with stray spaces and inconsistent case, mixed date formats, mixed channel casing, a comma used as a decimal point, a space used as a thousands separator, a blank quantity, and a blank customer name. Eleven different spellings collapse to seven when trim runs, and to five real customers when proper-case runs — plus one blank name that only the customer key can resolve. And two more problems survive all of this, because they are not formatting problems at all. We will meet them at the quality gate. chapters.title_en: Statistics — description, sampling, inference
chapters.teaches: why the average misleads, sampling distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, A/B decisions.
chapters.prediction: "Which of these two numbers moves when I drag the outlier?"
chapters.failure_beat: deciding the threshold after seeing the data.
chapters.artifact: an experiment memo — question, metric, assumptions, uncertainty, decision.
chapters.narration_en: The first number anyone computes is the average, and it is the first one that misleads them. Drag this one basket from ninety to six hundred: the mean follows it obediently, the median does not move at all. One is a description of the middle, the other is a description of the middle that one customer can move on their own. So describe the shape — centre, spread, skew and outliers — not a single number. Now the harder idea. You almost never measure everyone; you measure a sample. Take repeated samples from this population and watch their averages stack into a distribution of their own. That distribution is why statistics works, and it is also why a single sample average is not the truth. A confidence interval is a claim about the *procedure*: build a ninety-five percent interval a hundred times and roughly ninety-five of them will contain the real value. Watch the counter — it converges on ninety-five, and the ones that miss are drawn in red rather than hidden. A hypothesis test asks a narrower question: is this difference bigger than the noise I would expect anyway? And an A/B decision needs three things before you start, not after: the effect size worth acting on, the power you want, and therefore the sample size you need. Deciding those after seeing the data is how people convince themselves of things that are not there.

chapters.title_en: Semantic models, measures and the report
chapters.teaches: filter context, one definition per KPI, encoding chosen by question, accessibility as a floor.
chapters.prediction: "Why does % of total show 100 % everywhere?"
chapters.artifact: a one-page report spec with expected numbers a learner can check their build against.
chapters.narration_en: A chart is the last five percent of the work. Everything that makes it trustworthy sits behind it in the model. Relationships say how tables connect. A measure is not a column — it is a function evaluated against whatever rows survive the current filter context. Watch: the same measure returns a different number under each slicer, and nothing about the formula changed. That is why percentage-of-total breaks the first time you write it: the denominator is being filtered along with the numerator, so it always returns one hundred percent. It works when the denominator deliberately ignores the filter. Time intelligence is the same trap in a different costume — a same-period-last-year calculation *replaces* the date filter rather than narrowing it, and if you do not know that, your year-over-year comparison is quietly comparing a period with itself. The discipline that matters most here is one definition per KPI, defined once in the model and reused, instead of the same formula retyped slightly differently in four dashboards. And the report itself: choose the encoding from the question, not from the chart menu. Position for comparison, length for magnitude, colour for category and never for quantity. Check the contrast with the real formula, not by eye — this pairing measures twenty-one to one, and a surprising number of corporate palettes measure below three.

chapters.title_en: Software craft — design, refactoring, review
chapters.teaches: cohesion and coupling, SOLID as answers to real problems, safe refactoring, reading unfamiliar code, the ADR.
chapters.prediction: "How many files does this one change touch?"
chapters.failure_beat: the refactor step that reddens a test.
chapters.artifact: a refactor PR with identical behaviour and one ADR.
chapters.narration_en: Software craft is the difference between code that works today and a system somebody can change next year. Start with a measurement, not a slogan. Here is one change request, and here is the call graph lighting up six files that have to be touched to satisfy it. That is coupling, and you can see it. Split the module along its actual responsibilities and the same change touches one file. That is cohesion, and you can see that too. SOLID is not five commandments; it is five recurring pains with names attached. Put a policy behind an interface and you can swap it without editing the caller — that is dependency inversion earning its keep, not reciting itself. Refactoring means changing structure without changing behaviour, which is only safe if something is holding the behaviour still. That something is the test suite. Watch: small step, tests green; small step, tests green; small step, test red — so revert that one and think again. Without tests, refactoring is just rewriting and hoping. Then review. A good review reads the diff against the acceptance criteria and asks about correctness, edge cases, security and the next reader, and a good comment explains the impact rather than stating a preference. And every significant decision leaves an architecture decision record: what we chose, what we rejected, and what it will cost us. A design with no discarded option is a design nobody actually made.

chapters.teaches: the container defines the algorithm; Big-O as counted operations; graphs, traversal, topological order, shortest path.

chapters.narration_en: Algorithms are easier to feel than to memorise, provided you count the operations on screen instead of writing a table at the end. Linear search reads until it finds; binary search halves the space each time. Sixteen comparisons against four. On sixteen items that is a shrug. On a million items it is the difference between a page that loads and a page that does not. A hash table gives you constant-time lookup on average, and that phrase *on average* is doing real work: collisions are not an edge case, they are the normal case, and the load factor is the number that decides when the whole table has to be rebuilt. Now the sentence worth taking away from this chapter: the container defines the algorithm. Breadth-first search is a queue, so it explores level by level and finds the fewest hops. Depth-first search is a stack, so it dives. Dijkstra is a priority queue, so it always expands the cheapest frontier node and finds the cheapest path — thirteen, here. Watch the frontier and the visited set beside the graph and the behaviour stops being something to remember. And this matters far beyond interviews: a topological sort over a directed acyclic graph is exactly how an orchestrator decides what may run next. Add one edge that closes a cycle and the whole schedule becomes impossible — which is precisely the error Airflow gives you, a few chapters from now.

chapters.title_en: Networks, HTTP, APIs, identity and security
chapters.teaches: DNS → TCP → TLS → HTTP, API contracts, authn vs authz, and the OWASP failures you can see.
chapters.prediction: "The token is valid. Will this request succeed?"
chapters.artifact: `openapi.yaml`, contract tests, and a security write-up naming the three vulnerabilities found and fixed.
chapters.narration_en: Every service call starts as a name that is not an address. DNS resolves it, and then your message is cut into packets, each routed independently — which is why a network can lose one and not the others. TCP builds reliability on top of that unreliability with sequence numbers and acknowledgements, and TLS adds a second handshake for identity and encryption. That is why a cold connection is three and a half times slower than a warm one, and why connection reuse is one of the highest-value things a client can do. Then HTTP. A method, a path, headers, a body, and a status code — and status codes are not trivia. Four-oh-one says I do not know who you are. Four-oh-three says I know exactly who you are and you still may not. Four-twenty-nine says slow down. Five hundred says the fault is mine, not yours. Those four sentences tell you who has to fix the problem, which is the entire point of learning them. An API contract is the promise around all of that: validated inputs, explicit error shapes, pagination, idempotency, versioning — written down in a specification rather than living in one developer's head. Then identity. Authentication asks who you are; authorisation asks what you may do — and this is the single most common serious vulnerability in real systems. Watch: I change the identifier in the URL and read an order that is not mine. The token was valid the whole time. The check that was missing was not *are you logged in*, it was *is this yours*.

chapters.title_en: ETL, ELT and data quality
chapters.teaches: extract → validate → transform → load, the six quality dimensions run against live rows, and quarantine.
labels_en: completeness · uniqueness · validity · timeliness · consistency · accuracy
chapters.prediction: "The data is clean. How many checks fail?"

chapters.narration_en: A pipeline is the same record travelling from a source to a consumer, and everything interesting happens at the hops. Extract from a file, an API or a database. Then validate — before any large transformation, because transforming bad data just produces expensive bad data. The checks are boring and they are the job: does the schema match, are the types right, are mandatory fields present, are there duplicates, do the keys resolve, are the values in range, does the count match what the source said it sent. Now six quality dimensions, computed live against the real rows rather than asserted in a slide. Completeness, uniqueness, validity, timeliness, consistency, accuracy. And here is something deliberately left in: this clean, seeded dataset still fails two checks. One row points at a customer who does not exist, and one row carries a status outside the declared domain. Neither was injected by a demo button — they are genuinely in the data. A real quality gate finds a pre-existing defect on its first run, and widening the rule to make the gate green would have been the wrong fix. ETL transforms before loading; ELT loads raw and transforms inside the warehouse. The choice is about compute, governance, latency and platform, not fashion. And whatever fails, quarantine it with its reason attached. A row you silently dropped is a number that will be wrong downstream with nobody able to say why.

chapters.title_en: DAG orchestration, retries and idempotency
chapters.teaches: tasks and dependencies, retries with backoff, why retries demand idempotency, backfills, gates, lineage.
chapters.prediction: "The retry succeeded. Is the data correct?"
chapters.callback: the cycle from CH-19; pipes from CH-04.

chapters.narration_en: An orchestrator turns a pile of scripts into a graph with a promise attached: this runs after that, and nothing runs in a circle. Remember the topological sort from a few chapters ago — this is where it lives. Fail one task and watch carefully: only its descendants are affected. The unrelated branch keeps running, because the graph knows what actually depended on what. Retries look like the obvious answer, and here is the trap that defines this whole discipline. The task failed after it had already written half its rows. The retry runs it again from the top, it succeeds — and the row count is now double. The recovery caused the corruption. So a retry is only safe if the task is idempotent: running it twice produces the same result as running it once. Give the load a batch identifier and make it delete-then-insert for that batch, and now you can run it as many times as you like. That property is not a nicety; it is the thing that makes automated recovery possible at all. Backfills are the same problem with a calendar attached — reprocess history without overwriting data that is fresher than what you are replaying. And the last idea is the one that separates a pipeline from a plumbing exercise: put a quality gate before the publish step. If the counts do not reconcile, the gate short-circuits and yesterday's report stays up. Green tasks are not success. Correct, complete, fresh numbers are success.

chapters.title_en: Warehouse layers, star schema, OLAP and DataCube
chapters.teaches: ODS / ADS / warehouse / marts, facts and dimensions and grain, SCD, the cube operations, and the DataCube platform shape.

chapters.narration_en: A warehouse is not one database, it is layers with different jobs. The operational data store sits close to the source and keeps its shape. The warehouse integrates sources and keeps history. The application or curated layer serves analysis. Marts bring a domain close to the people who ask about it. Separating those is what makes debugging and ownership possible — ingestion is not storage, storage is not the semantic layer, and presentation is not governance. Inside the warehouse, the shape that has survived thirty years: a fact table in the middle, dimensions around it. The fact holds measures and foreign keys at one declared grain, and the grain is written on the table, not assumed. Dimensions describe. A cube is a group-by you can walk around. Roll up from month to quarter and the grid goes from eighteen cells to six, with three times as many rows behind each one. Click a cell and the scope narrows from two hundred and sixteen rows to seventy-two. Slice removes a plane; dice selects a sub-cube. And a warning that costs companies real money: average order value is not additive. You cannot average the averages — you compute total over total, per cell, every time. Then history. A July fact must join to July's customer tier, not today's. That is a slowly changing dimension, and getting it wrong rewrites the past silently. Finally: when a KPI is wrong, do not edit the formula. Trace it backwards — dashboard, measure, mart, warehouse, transformation, ingestion, source. The lineage graph is the difference between fixing a number and fixing a cause.

chapters.title_en: Hadoop — HDFS, YARN and MapReduce
chapters.teaches: blocks and replication, why compute travels to data, map-shuffle-reduce, and the ecosystem as history.

chapters.narration_en: When a file is larger than one machine, you split it. HDFS cuts it into blocks and scatters them across DataNodes, keeping several copies of each block on different machines and ideally different racks. The NameNode holds the map — which block lives where — and never touches your data, which is why losing it is a metadata catastrophe and not a data one. Kill a DataNode and watch: the file is still readable from the surviving replicas, and the cluster quietly starts making new copies to restore the replication factor. That is fault tolerance as motion rather than as a sentence on a slide. The second idea is the one that changed the industry: move the computation to the data, not the data to the computation, because moving terabytes across a network is the expensive part. MapReduce is the shape that came from it. Map produces key-value pairs locally. Shuffle sends every pair with the same key to the same place — and that arrow is the network, which is why shuffle is the moment to watch. Reduce produces the totals. Spark replaced the implementation but not the shape, which is why this is still worth ninety seconds. And the ecosystem around it — Sqoop, Flume, Oozie, ZooKeeper, Tez, Ambari, Hive, HBase — belongs on a timeline with an honest verdict each: what it solved, what replaced it, and whether you would reach for it today.

chapters.title_en: Spark — stages, partitions, shuffle and skew
chapters.teaches: lazy evaluation, the DAG cut into stages at shuffle boundaries, partitions as the unit of parallelism, skew.
chapters.prediction: "199 tasks are done, one is not. Will more machines help?"
chapters.artifact: a tuning report with before/after wall-clock for each of the three fixes.
chapters.narration_en: Spark is lazy on purpose. You chain transformations and nothing runs — it is building a graph of what you asked for. Only when you call an action does it plan and execute, and that delay is what lets it optimise across the whole chain instead of one step at a time. The scheduler cuts that graph into stages, and it cuts exactly where a shuffle is required. A narrow transformation keeps each partition independent; a wide one has to move data between machines, and that is a stage boundary. So when someone asks you to read a Spark plan, the skill is not naming operators — it is pointing at where the shuffles are and saying why. A partition is the unit of work. Too few and most of your cluster is idle. Too many and you pay scheduling overhead on thousands of tiny tasks. Now the failure that looks exactly like a slow cluster and is not. Two hundred tasks finish quickly, and one keeps going. Every other executor is idle while a single bar climbs. That is skew: one key is far larger than the rest, so one task got most of the data. Adding machines does nothing at all, because the problem is distribution, not capacity. Repartition, or salt the hot key, or broadcast the small side of the join so there is no shuffle to skew. And notice that this lands us back where SQL tuning did: performance starts with the shape of the data and the plan, not with a bigger machine.

chapters.title_en: Kafka and near-real-time streaming
chapters.teaches: topics, partitions, offsets, consumer groups, lag, ordering scope, delivery semantics, schema evolution.
chapters.prediction: "It crashed after processing. What happens on restart?"
chapters.failure_beat: the duplicate; the incompatible schema change.
chapters.artifact: a consumer with an idempotent sink and a documented delivery guarantee.
chapters.narration_en: Kafka is not a database with a different name. It is a log: producers append events to the end, consumers read forward, and events stay for a retention window whether anyone has read them or not. A topic is split into partitions, and here is the fact that decides your design: ordering is guaranteed within a partition, not across the topic. If two events must be processed in order, they must share a key so they land in the same partition. Each consumer keeps an offset — the position it has reached — and you can watch that marker move rather than take the word on trust. A consumer group shares the partitions out; add a consumer and the group rebalances, and during that rebalance latency wobbles, which is worth knowing before it happens in production. Lag is the distance between the last available offset and the last processed one, and lag is the single most useful number in a streaming system — but only when you can see its cause in the same frame, which here is a slow sink downstream. Now delivery. The consumer processed the message and then crashed before committing the offset. On restart it processes the same message again. Exactly-once is a property of the whole path, not a Kafka setting — the practical answer is at-least-once delivery into a sink that is idempotent, which is the same word that saved us in the DAG chapter. And when the schema changes: adding a field with a default is compatible; removing a field consumers require is not, and the registry should refuse it before it reaches anyone.

chapters.title_en: Mobile Money — one transaction end to end
chapters.teaches: the NilePay transaction's journey, event time vs ingestion time vs processing time, the freshness SLO, ODS → ADS → report.
chapters.prediction: "The report is 11 minutes stale. Which hop?"
chapters.artifact: an NRT freshness timeline with the SLO drawn on it.
chapters.narration_en: Let us follow one transaction with a fixed identifier, all the way through. A customer sends money. The operational system records the amount, both parties, a timestamp, a status and a transaction identifier — and that identifier is the thread we hold for the next two minutes. The event enters the streaming path, then lands in the operational data store, which stays close to the source deliberately. At every hop, stamp four clocks: when the business event happened, when the platform received it, when it was processed, and when it became available to a report. Those are four different times, and treating them as one is the single most common cause of numbers that look wrong to a business user who was there when it happened. After validation and transformation, the curated layer gives it business structure: a fact tied to time, customer, service, channel and region. Now the callback that makes the whole architecture legible — here is the same transaction identifier, glowing in a dashboard tile. Not a similar example. The same event. Every layer is talking about one thing. And when the freshness objective breaks — when the report is older than five minutes — the timeline tells you exactly which hop absorbed the delay: ingestion, processing, or the downstream load. That is the difference between near-real-time as a measurement and near-real-time as a word in a proposal. And these six rows should look familiar. They are the receipts we started with.

chapters.title_en: Reconciliation, governance, DR and compliance
chapters.teaches: the four mismatch classes, why a net total lies, acceptance testing, masking and k-anonymity, RPO/RTO, multi-tenancy.
chapters.prediction: "Net difference is €66. Is that one fault or several?"
chapters.failure_beat: the cancelling faults; k = 1 after masking.
chapters.artifact: a reconciliation report by break class plus an acceptance-evidence pack.
chapters.narration_en: Reconciliation is proving that two systems agree about the same financial truth, and it is the work that makes every other number in this film trustworthy. Compare the switch file against the core ledger. Seven records match. Then four different kinds of break, and they are not one problem: an amount mismatch of thirty-six — and notice thirty-six is divisible by nine, which is the classic signature of two transposed digits, so that is a data-entry or parsing fault, not a money fault. One transaction present only in the switch. One present only in the ledger. And one duplicate. Now the sentence to take away. The net difference is sixty-six euros. If you had reconciled on a single net total you would have seen a small, almost acceptable gap — because three unrelated faults partly cancelled each other out. A net total is not a reconciliation. Matching at the record level is. The same honesty applies to privacy. Remove every direct identifier from this table and re-identification risk is still one — nine rows are each alone in their class. Generalise country and decade and some rows are still alone. Only suppression gets you to a group of at least two. Masking a name is where protection starts, not where it ends. Then the delivery layer: acceptance testing that ties each checklist item to evidence rather than the word *passed*; a risk board that names impact, owner and mitigation; and disaster recovery expressed as two numbers — how much data you can afford to lose, and how long you can afford to be down. Fail the site and measure them, because an untested recovery plan is a document, not a capability.

chapters.title_en: Machine learning from a business question
chapters.teaches: baseline first, features and labels, the split, leakage, and error measured on data the model never saw.
chapters.prediction: "This model scores 0.99. Good or suspicious?"
chapters.artifact: a model experiment record — baseline, split, metric, result, failure cases, decision.
chapters.narration_en: Machine learning starts with a business question and a baseline, not with an algorithm. If a simple rule or a SQL query answers the question well enough, a model is not automatically better — it is just harder to explain and more expensive to operate. So write the baseline down and score it. Sixty-five and a half, mean absolute error. Now thirty houses we have sold. An estate agent's rule of thumb draws a line that misses at both ends. A fitted line pivots into place through the evidence, minimising the distance to the points, and it scores seven point three three — on data it has never seen. That last clause is the whole discipline. You do not judge a model on the examples it learned from; you judge it on held-out data, because a model that memorises scores perfectly and knows nothing. Which brings us to leakage, the failure that produces the most impressive wrong results in this field. Three kinds. A column that would not exist yet at prediction time. A feature quietly derived from the answer. And rows from the same group appearing in both training and test, so the model recognises the group rather than learning the pattern. Each one produces a score that looks like a triumph and collapses in production. Split by group, and the honest number appears. And one discipline that people skip: tune on validation, and open the test set once. Every extra look at the test set is a small amount of fitting to it that you cannot see and cannot undo.

chapters.title_en: Model families and evaluation depth
chapters.teaches: four shapes of ruler, the metric that matches the cost, thresholds, cross-validation, bias and variance.
chapters.prediction: "99 % accurate. Is it any good?"
chapters.artifact: a model card with metric, threshold rationale and error analysis.
chapters.narration_en: There are four shapes of ruler and the question chooses between them, not fashion. A linear model draws a straight boundary and is easy to explain. A tree splits on thresholds and handles interactions naturally but is unstable on its own. Ensembles average many trees and are usually the strongest thing you will fit on tabular data. Distance-based methods assume nearness means similarity, which is fine until you have many columns. Pick before you fit, using rows per parameter: a flexible model on a small dataset will learn noise with great confidence. Then evaluation, and the trap everyone meets once. This classifier is ninety-nine percent accurate — and the confusion matrix shows it caught none of the cases you built it for, because only one percent of the data is positive and predicting *no* every time scores ninety-nine. So use precision when a false alarm is expensive, recall when a miss is expensive, and F1 when you need one number. The threshold is not a statistical choice, it is a business one: move it and watch the cost in pounds swap between false positives and false negatives. Cross-validation gives you a more stable estimate by rotating the held-out fold — and it must keep groups intact, or you have rebuilt the leak from the last chapter inside your evaluation. Finally, bias and variance. Increase the polynomial degree: training error keeps falling while test error turns back upward. That turning point is overfitting, visible rather than defined.

chapters.title_en: Neural networks — neuron to backpropagation
chapters.teaches: a neuron as a weighted sum, a layer, the forward pass, loss, the chain rule, one weight update.
chapters.prediction: "Double the learning rate. Faster, or broken?"
chapters.callback: gradient descent previewed in CH-16's fitting.

chapters.narration_en: A neuron is a weighted sum with an opinion about zero. Multiply each input by a weight, add a bias, and pass the result through an activation function. Every number in that sentence is on screen, computed on one real customer — there is nothing hidden inside the box. The activation matters more than it looks: without a nonlinearity, stacking layers gives you nothing, because a linear function of a linear function is still a linear function. The bend is what lets a network represent something a straight line cannot. A layer is just neurons sharing the same inputs, and a network is layers reading each other's outputs. Count the parameters yourself rather than being told the number — that is where the size of a model actually comes from. Now the part that sounds mystical and is not. Run the forward pass, get a prediction, and measure how wrong it is: that is the loss. Then ask a question you can answer with the chain rule: if I nudged this one weight, how would the loss change? That is the gradient — a slope with a sign. Step the weight in the direction that reduces the loss, a little. Do it again. That is training. And the step size is not a detail: watch the loss descend smoothly, then raise the learning rate past roughly zero point three five and watch it diverge on screen, because the arithmetic genuinely diverges. Every model in the rest of this film is this loop, repeated at scale.

chapters.narration_en: Text has to become numbers before anything can happen to it. First tokens: not words, not letters — pieces, chosen by frequency, which is why a rare word costs several tokens and a common one costs a single token. Then each token identifier becomes a vector, and position is added, because attention on its own has no idea what order anything came in. Now the mechanism the whole field is built on, small enough to follow every number: eight dimensions, two heads, one block, six hundred and ninety-six weights, and every one of them is multiplied on screen. Each token produces three projections — a query, a key and a value. The query of the token we are looking at is compared against the key of every token, producing a grid of raw scores. Then the causal mask greys out the future, because a model predicting the next token must not be allowed to read ahead. Then softmax turns the remaining scores into weights, and notice that every row sums to exactly one — it is a distribution over what to pay attention to. The values are blended by those weights and written into the residual stream, which is the thing every block reads from and writes back to. Stack blocks, and at the end the model produces a distribution over the next token. Not an answer — a distribution. Temperature flattens or sharpens it; top-p truncates its tail. Neither adds knowledge. Sample one token, append it, and run the whole stack again. That is generation.

chapters.narration_en: An embedding turns text into a position, and nearby positions mean similar things. That is the whole trick behind semantic search: keyword search matches strings, embeddings match meaning, and cosine similarity is how you ask which is nearest. Retrieval-augmented generation is a pipeline, and every stage can fail on its own. Documents are split into chunks. Chunks are embedded and indexed. A query retrieves candidates. An access filter removes what this user may not see. A reranker reorders. The survivors become context. The model answers, with citations. And here is a measured failure rather than a claimed one. Ask *how do I stop a job loading the same rows twice*. The top hit is a roadmap section scoring zero point one six five — confident, wrong and weak. Expand the query with synonyms and the idempotency section climbs to zero point two two seven and takes the top slot. That is vocabulary mismatch, and it is why most RAG failures are retrieval failures, not generation failures. Now the security sentence worth memorising: retrieval is a query, not a permission. A chunk can be semantically perfect and still be something this user must never see, so the filter belongs at the retrieval layer — before the model, not after it, because once text is in the context window it has already leaked. Finally, agents. An agent is not a longer chatbot. It is a loop: a goal, a state, a tool chosen, an observation, an updated state, and a stop condition. Every dangerous step passes a policy check first. Watch a generated `DELETE` meet an allowlist that rejects the statement type, and then a read-only database role that would have rejected it anyway. Two independent layers, because one is a promise and two is a design.

chapters.narration_en: A container is the answer to *it works on my machine*: the application and its dependencies packaged so the environment travels with the code. Images are built in layers and cached, and the order of your Dockerfile is therefore an economic decision. Change one source line with a sensible layer order and the rebuild costs five seconds. Move the copy of your source code above the dependency install and the identical change costs fifty-seven, every single time, for the rest of the project's life. Continuous integration runs the build, the tests and the scans on every commit, and a gate that never blocks anything is decoration — watch a failing test stop the release, and watch the pipeline say which test and why. Deployment is not finished when the code is out; it is finished when you have a health check that can tell you it went wrong and a rollback that can take you back. In the cloud, the rule that surprises people: an explicit deny always wins. Attach a wildcard administrator policy alongside a deny and nothing changes — read the evaluation trace and you can see every statement that was consulted. Then operations. Three signals: logs tell you what happened, metrics tell you how much and how often, traces tell you where the time went — and they are only useful together, joined by one correlation identifier that follows a request across every service. Here is the incident. The p95 is climbing and the error rate is completely flat, which is the fingerprint of a saturating resource rather than a bug. Symptom, signal, hypothesis, evidence, root cause, fix, validation, and a regression check so it cannot come back silently. The output is a written incident report and a runbook entry, not a restart.

chapters.narration_en: What you carry out of all this is not a certificate. It is a chain. Thirteen artifacts, each one generated from the one before it: the messy export becomes the cleaned file, the cleaned file becomes the database seed, the seed is what the queries run against, the queries feed the model, the model defines the measures, the measures produce the report, and the scripts and tests reproduce the whole thing on somebody else's machine. That word *chain* is a claim about lineage, not a folder of related files — and the test is simple. Change one cell in the raw export and watch every downstream artifact move with it. If they do not move, you had a collection, not a chain. Now a distinction this film will not blur. Completing something and proving something are two different numbers and they are never added together. Ticking a lesson is a note you wrote about yourself. Evidence is a repository a stranger can clone and run, a test suite that fails on a real bug, a query plan with a measured before and after, a pipeline that produces identical counts when run twice, a dashboard, an incident report. Then the defence: five minutes, four sections — the problem, the architecture, a working demonstration, and the trade-offs. Most people rush the fourth one, and the fourth one is the only part that is hard. A component you cannot justify is a component you have not designed, so for every box on your diagram, know the simpler alternative you rejected and why. And then choose a branch — backend, data engineering, analytics engineering, machine learning, platform, or mobile money. One project, one graph, six destinations.

chapters.narration_ar: اللي هتطلع بيه من ده كله مش شهادة. ده سلسلة. تلتاشر artifact، كل واحد متولّد من اللي قبله: الملف المبعثر بيبقى الملف المنضّف، والمنضّف بيبقى بذرة الـdatabase، والبذرة هي اللي الـqueries بتشتغل عليها، والـqueries بتغذّي الـmodel، والـmodel بيعرّف الـmeasures، والـmeasures بتنتج التقرير، والـscripts والـtests بيعيدوا إنتاج ده كله على جهاز حد تاني. وكلمة *سلسلة* دي دعوى عن الـlineage، مش folder فيه ملفات قرايب — والاختبار بسيط. غيّر خلية واحدة في الملف الخام وبصّ على كل artifact بعده وهو بيتحرك معاها. لو ما اتحركوش، يبقى كان عندك مجموعة مش سلسلة. ودلوقتي تفرقة الفيديو ده مش هيميّعها. إنك تخلّص حاجة وإنك تثبت حاجة دول رقمين مختلفين وعمرهم ما بيتجمعوا. إنك تعلّم على درس دي ملاحظة كتبتها عن نفسك. أما الدليل فهو repo حد غريب يقدر يعمل له clone ويشغّله، وtest suite بتفشل على bug حقيقي، وquery plan معاه قياس قبل وبعد، وpipeline بتطلع نفس الأعداد لما تشتغل مرتين، وdashboard، وتقرير حادث. بعدها الدفاع: خمس دقايق، أربع أقسام — المشكلة، والمعمار، وعرض شغال، والـtrade-offs. وأغلب الناس بتستعجل الرابع، والرابع هو الجزء الصعب الوحيد. والمكوّن اللي مش قادر تبرّره هو مكوّن ما صمّمتوش، فلكل مربع في الرسمة بتاعتك، اعرف البديل الأبسط اللي رفضته وليه. وبعدها اختار مسار — backend أو data engineering أو analytics engineering أو machine learning أو platform أو mobile money. مشروع واحد، graph واحد، ست وجهات.

chapters.narration_en: Here is the whole thing, lit. Every component you watched arrive, in the order you met it. And here is what you actually learned, which is not the diagram — it is this wall. The retry that duplicated the data. The two sessions deadlocked over two rows. The one hot key that idled a cluster. The model that scored ninety-nine percent and caught nothing. The chunk that was perfectly relevant and completely unauthorised. Every one of those looked correct until someone looked properly. That is the job. Not knowing the names of tools, but being the person who asks *what happens when this runs twice*, and *one row per what*, and *what would I have to see to know I was wrong*. And it still comes back to a shoebox of receipts and a question somebody actually needs answered. Get the rows. Make them trustworthy. Answer the question. Everything else is scale.
